content: 1. The proportion of children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) who were treated with ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) in an outpatient setting over an 8-week period was evaluated. 2. Outcomes for severely malnourished children with edema treated in outpatient care were assessed. 3. In a study by Ciliberto (2006), outcomes for children with edema but no wasting treated in outpatient therapeutic programs (OTP) showed a recovery rate of 95%, a mortality rate of 4%, a default rate of 1%, and a failure rate of 1%. 4. For children with edema and no wasting treated in OTP, the median weight gain (interquartile range) was reported. 5. Among children who began home care with edema (80% of cases), the mortality rate was 0%, and the recovery rate was 100% for both edema and non-edema cases. 6. Some cases of mortality were attributed to tuberculosis or the need for blood transfusion. 7. Outcomes for children with SAM and edema (98% of cases) treated exclusively in outpatient settings (77% of cases) were not reported separately. 8. Mortality (4%), defaulting (3%), failure (8%), and transfer (2%) rates were reported only for the global group, which included children with kwashiorkor, marasmus, or both. 9. A comparison of outcomes for different treatment approaches showed varying mortality rates, but specific data on deaths and predicted numbers were not consistently reported. 10. Default rates in global studies of moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) and SAM were analyzed, with statistical significance noted for all comparisons. 11. Retrospective studies on uncomplicated SAM treated with RUTF in outpatient settings often did not report outcomes for edema cases. 12. A review of 33 guidelines on community-based management of acute malnutrition (CMAM) across various countries highlighted differences in the inclusion of edema cases in outpatient care. 13. Key terms used in database searches for studies on nutritional edema included kwashiorkor, malnutrition and edema, and community care. 14. Several studies were excluded from analysis due to lack of data on the prevalence or outcomes of edema cases, small sample sizes, or focus on inpatient care. 15. Reviews and trials on community-based management of SAM often did not report specific outcomes for children with edema treated in outpatient settings. 16. Studies comparing inpatient, outpatient, and combined treatment approaches frequently excluded edema cases from outpatient groups or failed to report their outcomes. 17. Research on dietary regimens for malnourished children often focused on inpatient stabilization and did not provide data on edema outcomes during outpatient phases. 18. Evaluations of community-based therapeutic care models for SAM highlighted differences in triage criteria and treatment settings for children with varying degrees of edema. 19. Reviews on the causes of mortality in SAM treatment emphasized the need for better reporting and management of edema cases. 20. Studies on domiciliary management of kwashiorkor and other forms of malnutrition often lacked data on main outcomes or focused on small sample sizes. 21. Research on the cost-effectiveness of community-based treatment for SAM highlighted the potential benefits but often lacked specific data on edema cases. 22. Reviews on the efficacy of community-based treatment approaches for SAM frequently omitted data on the prevalence and outcomes of edema cases. 23. Studies on the use of local food resources or specific therapeutic foods for malnutrition rehabilitation often did not report outcomes for children with edema. 24. Research on supplementary feeding programs and ambulatory care for malnourished children often excluded or failed to report on edema cases. 25. Evaluations of home-based therapy with RUTF during food crises highlighted its benefits but lacked detailed data on edema outcomes. 26. Studies on the management of SAM in high HIV prevalence areas often focused on inpatient stabilization and did not report outcomes for edema cases during outpatient care. 27. Reviews on the management of acute malnutrition in resource-poor settings emphasized the need for better data on edema prevalence and outcomes. 28. Research on the use of mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) for nutritional programming provided evidence for new approaches but did not focus on edema outcomes. 29. Studies on the causes of mortality in SAM treatment highlighted the need for improved management of edema cases to reduce mortality rates. 30. Research on the use of RUTF with varying milk content for SAM treatment showed differences in effectiveness but did not focus on edema outcomes. 31. Evaluations of community-based therapeutic care models for SAM in sub-Saharan Africa highlighted the need for consistent reporting of edema outcomes. 32. Studies on the management of SAM in emergency relief programs often lacked data on edema prevalence and outcomes. 33. Research on the routine use of antibiotics in home-based SAM treatment highlighted its benefits but did not report specific outcomes for edema cases. 34. Reviews on the cost-effectiveness of community-based SAM treatment emphasized its potential but often lacked data on edema outcomes. 35. Studies on the use of local food resources for malnutrition rehabilitation often did not report outcomes for children with edema. 36. Research on the management of SAM in rural settings often lacked data on edema prevalence and outcomes. 37. Reviews on the causes of high mortality rates in SAM treatment emphasized the need for better management of edema cases. 38. Studies on domiciliary management of kwashiorkor often lacked data on main outcomes or focused on small sample sizes. 39. Research on ambulatory care for malnourished children often excluded or failed to report on edema cases. 40. Evaluations of community-based therapeutic care models for SAM highlighted the need for consistent reporting of edema outcomes.
